nodes.label: Mountain navigation
nodes.answer: Use a paper map and compass together with GPS or a phone app, but never rely on electronics alone. Plan the route in advance, track your position against terrain features, and know when to turn back.

nodes.label: Topographic map
nodes.answer: Carry a current topographic paper map and learn its scale, legend, contour lines, and grid system. A map shows the wider terrain and escape options that a small phone screen can easily hide.

nodes.label: Map legend
nodes.answer: Read the map legend before setting out so you understand trails, water, cliffs, vegetation, buildings, and contour intervals. Map symbols differ between map publishers and countries.

nodes.label: Map scale
nodes.answer: Use the map scale to convert map distance into real-world distance. For example, on a 1:25,000 map, 4 centimeters represents 1 kilometer on the ground.

nodes.label: Contour lines
nodes.answer: Contour lines show elevation and terrain shape. Closely spaced contours mean steep ground, while V- or U-shaped contours can indicate valleys and re-entrants; use them to anticipate cliffs, ridges, and difficult descents.

nodes.label: Terrain features
nodes.answer: Learn to recognize peaks, ridges, spurs, valleys, re-entrants, saddles, cliffs, and watercourses on both the map and the ground. Matching visible terrain to the map is one of the most reliable ways to confirm your location.

nodes.label: Compass
nodes.answer: A compass works without batteries and is essential for taking bearings, orienting the map, and navigating in poor visibility. Learn to use it with a paper map before you need it in an emergency.

nodes.label: Compass basics
nodes.answer: Learn the main compass parts: magnetic needle, rotating bezel, orienting arrow and lines, direction-of-travel arrow, and baseplate. Practice taking and following bearings in familiar terrain before relying on them in mountains.

nodes.label: Taking a bearing
nodes.answer: To take a bearing, align the compass baseplate between your position and destination on the map, rotate the bezel to match north, apply declination if needed, then follow the direction-of-travel arrow on the ground. Use intermediate landmarks and check the bearing regularly.

nodes.label: Magnetic declination
nodes.answer: Magnetic declination is the angle between true or grid north and magnetic north. Apply the correct local correction when converting between map bearings and compass bearings, or set the compass declination in advance.

nodes.label: Orienting the map
nodes.answer: Orient the map so its north aligns with north on the ground, using visible landmarks or your compass. A correctly oriented map makes it much easier to match terrain features and choose the correct route.

nodes.label: GPS navigation
nodes.answer: Use GPS for position, tracks, and waypoints, but carry a map and compass as backup. Batteries can fail, screens can become unreadable in cold or rain, and satellite reception can be poor in deep valleys or dense forest.

nodes.label: Smartphone navigation
nodes.answer: Download offline maps before leaving, enable airplane mode to save battery, and carry a power bank. A phone is useful, but cold, rain, damage, or a dead battery can make it unavailable when you need it most.

nodes.label: Waypoints
nodes.answer: Mark key waypoints such as the trailhead, major junctions, water sources, camps, escape routes, and the summit. Waypoints help you navigate back, confirm progress, and find a safe exit if conditions change.

nodes.label: Route planning
nodes.answer: Plan the route in segments, noting distance, elevation gain, expected time, hazards, junctions, water sources, and escape options. Share the plan with someone reliable and set a firm turnaround time.

nodes.label: Route card
nodes.answer: A route card breaks a journey into legs with a start point, bearing, distance, time estimate, terrain description, and escape option. It is especially useful in poor visibility or on complex mountain terrain.

nodes.label: Handrails
nodes.answer: A handrail is a long, easy-to-follow feature such as a stream, ridge, trail, fence, road, or shoreline. Where possible, plan legs along handrails to reduce the chance of drifting off course.

nodes.label: Catching features
nodes.answer: A catching feature is an unmistakable feature beyond your destination that tells you that you have gone too far, such as a road, river, lake, or major ridge. Identify it before starting each navigation leg.

nodes.label: Attack point
nodes.answer: Use an attack point—a clear, easy-to-find feature near your destination—to simplify the final, more difficult leg. Navigate accurately to the attack point first, then take a short bearing or carefully follow terrain to the target.

nodes.label: Aiming off
nodes.answer: Aim slightly to one side of a linear feature so you know which direction to turn when you reach it. This technique reduces the chance of missing a trail, stream, or ridge in poor visibility.

nodes.label: Dead reckoning
nodes.answer: Dead reckoning estimates your position from a known starting point using bearing, distance, pace, and time. In fog, snow, or featureless terrain, combine it with careful compass work and frequent reality checks.

nodes.label: Pace counting
nodes.answer: Calibrate your normal pace count over a known distance, then use it to estimate how far you have traveled. Slope, snow, fatigue, wind, and heavy packs can change your pace, so treat it as an estimate rather than an exact measurement.

nodes.label: Timing and distance
nodes.answer: Estimate hiking time from distance, elevation gain, terrain, fitness, pack weight, and breaks. Build in extra time for navigation, poor weather, and rest, and use timing to notice when you may have missed a feature.

nodes.label: Poor visibility navigation
nodes.answer: In fog, whiteout, or darkness, slow down, use a compass bearing, follow handrails, and use catching features to prevent overshooting. If you cannot maintain an accurate position, stop safely or retreat by the route you know.

nodes.label: Getting lost
nodes.answer: If you become unsure of your position, stop before making the error worse. Use the STOP method—Stop, Think, Observe, Plan—retrace to your last known point if safe, and call for help early if conditions or daylight are deteriorating.

nodes.label: Retracing a route
phrases: go back the way you came
nodes.answer: Retracing is often safer than continuing into unfamiliar terrain, especially in poor weather or fading light. Use recorded tracks, waypoints, back bearings, and recognizable landmarks to return to a known position.

nodes.label: Navigation checkpoints
nodes.answer: Check your position regularly using a combination of terrain, compass bearing, distance or time, and GPS if available. Frequent small checks are safer than trying to relocate after you have traveled far off route.

nodes.label: Navigation equipment
nodes.answer: Carry a waterproof paper map, reliable compass, charged phone or GPS, power bank, watch, and headlamp. Keep electronics protected from cold and moisture, and know how to use every item without relying on mobile data.

nodes.label: Navigation practice
nodes.answer: Practice navigation regularly in familiar, low-risk terrain. Start with simple map-and-compass exercises, then gradually practice bearings, contour interpretation, and poor-visibility techniques before relying on them in mountains.
